senses.gloss:
maraṇa
(‘that which separates the आत्मन् form the body’)
------------------------------------------
Birth (janma) and death (maraṇa) have been an inscrutable mystery to man right from the most ancient days. In trying to solve this mystery, several theories have been put forward. If death is considered by some as total annihilation of the human personality, others accept the survival of a सोउल् after death, which goes to either हेअवेन् or हेल्ल्, eternally, depending upon its deeds done here. Both of them are, more or less, silent on what causes birth. The third view, as held by the Hindu sages, is that the सोउल् is eternally existing, having neither birth nor death. It is the body that is born. It is the body again, that dies. The सोउल् is made to incarnate in the body, by an eternal law of God, the kind of body, the duration of life and the various experiences in life being determined by the कर्म or the moral deserts of that सोउल्, carried over from the previous lives.
Every being that is born, has to die one day, the manner of death, again, depending upon the सोउल्’s कर्म.
Maraṇa or death can come to a person due to natural causes like old age or diseases, or, it can be caused by unnatural causes like accident, सुइचिदे, murder or capital punishment.
It is interesting to note that the Hindu scriptures describe certain signs as indicative of approaching death. Some of them are: not being able to see the star Arundhati (the small star Alcor) or the pole-star or the full-मोओन् even though there is perfect visibility; seeing the orb of the मोओन् or the sun with a hole in it; smelling the odour of a corpse even though fragrant substances are near; not hearing the humming or the internal noise when the ears are closed; not seeing one’s reflection in another’s eyes standing in front and so on.
Dreaming of an ass or an old maid or a trident also prognosticates imminent death.
The scriptures also stress the point that the last thought at the time of death, can determine the next birth (vide Bhagavadgītā 8.6).
Death, while fighting for dharma—as for instance, to protect a righteous person in danger—has been considered glorious.
Hindu scriptures have permitted reli-gious सुइचिदे in certain cases such as जीवन्मुक्ति (liberation even while living), decrepitude due to extreme old-age, incurable diseases causing unbearable suffering or as a प्रायश्चित्त (expiation) for heinous crimes.
See also ANTYEṢṬI, MṚTYU and YAMA.

Marudgaṇa
(‘the group of [gods] called Marut’)
------------------------------------------
There are many Vedic gods out of which the मरुद्गण or a group of Maruts is one. They are described by some modern scholars as the personification of storms. Their number is mentioned sometimes as 21 and sometimes as 180.
They are depicted as the sons of रुद्र and Pṛśni. They are handsome, fiery in colour and nature, and, live in the अन्तरिक्ष (intervening space between this earth and heavens). Lightning and thunderbolt are their weapons. Giving rains to us is one of their important duties. Though terrifying in appearance they are full of compassion towards their votaries. Several hymns of the Ṛgveda (vide 5.52-60) are in praise of them.
The epics contain an interesting story about them. When दिति, the मोथेर् of the दैत्यस् (demons), was pregnant, expecting a very powerful son as per the blessing of her husband कश्यप, इन्द्र, the king of gods, is said to have stealthily broken the foetus into 49 parts. These ‘babies’ started weeping. At the request of their मोथेर् दिति, इन्द्र granted them protection, godhood, and made them the controllers of wind (Mahābhārata, Ādiparva, 132).

Marīci
------------------------------------------
Considered a mānasaputra or मिन्द्-born son of ब्रह्मा, the creator, मरीचि, is reckoned among the prajāpatis (progenitors of mankind). He is also one of the सप्तर्षिस् (seven sages).
His wife was कला, the daughter of कर्दम, another प्रजापति. The sage कश्यप was his son.
There is a स्मृति attributed to him and its verses are quoted by other writers of धर्मशास्त्रस्.
His opinions on आह्निक (daily routine of a द्विज or the twice-born), अशौच (ceremonial impurity), śrāddha (obsequial rites), प्रायश्चित्त (expiations for sins) and vyavahāra (secular life) have been noted with respect.
Some of his views like the transactions involved in sale of property approach our modern laws.
The स्मृति perhaps, contained both verses and sentences in prose.

Mārkaṇḍeya
(‘son of the [sage] Mṛkaṇḍu’)
------------------------------------------
Destined to die at an early age, the young मार्कण्डेय worshipped Lord शिव with intense devotion to transcend death. Just as यम, the god of death, approached him with his noose, to take him away, मार्कण्डेय clung to the शिवलिङ्ग he was worshipping, whence शिव appeared with his trident and prevented him from doing so. He also gave मार्कण्डेय, a long life of 14 kalpas’ duration (a कल्प = one day of ब्रह्मा).
He is sometimes classed along the cirañjīvis (those who live eternally) along with हनुमान्, व्यास and others.
The Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa is attributed to him as the chief narrator.
He is said to be one of the smṛtikāras who edited and condensed the original Manusmṛti to 8000 ślokas and passed it on to Sumati भार्गव. मार्कण्डेय appears in the Mahābhārata as also in some पुराणस् like the Bhāgavata and the Matsya. He is said to have visited the Pāṇḍavas in the Kāmyakavana and taught them धर्म through many stories. He also told युधिष्ठिर that Śrī कृष्ण was the Supreme Lord Himself (Vanaparva 189).
While discussing धर्म with the sage नारद, मार्कण्डेय gives his views on various topics connected with मर्रिअगे and chastity (Mahābhārata, Anuśāsanaparva 50-62).
There is one मार्कण्डेय आश्रम near Bhāgeśvara at the confluence of the rivers गोमती and सरयू in Uttar Pradesh.

Mārttāṇḍa
(‘[born out of] dead egg’)
------------------------------------------
Mārttāṇḍa is one of the names of सूर्य, the Sun-god. Son of अदिति and कश्यप he is said to have been born dead but revived to life by the sage कश्यप.
Mārttāṇḍa—also spelt as Martand or Matan—is a place in Kashmir, about 50 kms. (31 miles) south-east of Srinagar. It is famous for its temple of Sun built by the king Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa (8th century A. D.). It was demolished by the Muslim Vandal Sikandar (14th century A. D.) Though in ruins, it is considered as one of the beautiful temples of Kashmir.
The temple is of a moderate size, 18.6 metres (60 ft.) by 11 metres (36 ft.). With two facades in the front, the width becomes 18.6 metres (60 ft.).
There is a courtyard of 68 metres (220 ft.) by 44 metres (142 ft.) surrounding the temple. Even in the state of ruin, it appears magnificent.
The roof is missing. The building is adorned with high relief carvings of themes relating to the cult of the Sun.

mārjana
(‘cleansing’)
------------------------------------------
The सन्ध्या ritual—also called ‘sandhyāvandana’—is an important part of the daily routine of every द्विज (a member of the first three castes). Out of the several steps involved in its performance, मार्जन is also one.
Mārjana is ceremonially purifying the body by sprinkling water with कुश grass (Poa cynosuroides retz) on specified parts of the body, with the repetition of the well-known Vedic मन्त्र ‘āpo hi ṣṭhā’ (Ṛgveda 10.9.1-3).
Sometimes the गायत्री मन्त्र along with the three व्याहृतिस् (bhūḥ etc.) as also some more Vedic mantras are also pres-cribed to be recited during मार्जन.
See also GĀYATRĪ and SANDHYĀ-VANDANA.
